opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't know for sure, and I think nobody really can before they actually do it. But I had some pretty strong signals.

During undergrad I'd already spent a lot of time on side projects, mostly computer graphics and physics simulation, things like writing my own renderers and little fluid solvers. Nobody asked me to do them, and there was no grade attached. I'd stay up late just because I wanted to see whether the smoke would look right or the simulation would stay stable. When you find yourself doing something voluntarily, again and again, even when it's frustrating, that's a good sign it's intrinsic motivation and not just something that looks good on a resume.

I also got some early research experience before applying, working with people on real problems where the answer wasn't in a textbook. That's different from coursework. In a class you know a solution exists. In research you often don't, and you spend weeks stuck. I noticed that I didn't hate being stuck. It was uncomfortable, but the moment things finally clicked felt so rewarding that it made the whole struggle worth it.

So my reasoning was: if I enjoy building things from scratch, I'm okay with uncertainty, and I'm excited about a specific field, then a PhD, which is basically five years of exactly that, probably fits me. I wouldn't say I was certain. It was more like I had enough evidence to make a reasonable bet. And I'd tell people considering a PhD to do the same: try small research projects first, and pay attention to how you feel when nothing is working, not just when things go well.

r001.rationale: The response describes Hu’s undergrad side projects, early research experience, and comfort with uncertainty, but does not characterize his transition as moving from reproducing others’ papers to creating his own.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't know. I think that's the first thing I'd say to anyone asking that question: I didn't have some certainty before I started.

What I did have was a few experiences during undergrad at Tsinghua that gave me a taste. I spent a lot of time in competitive programming before that, and I enjoyed it, but at some point I realized that competitions are about solving problems that someone else already knows the answer to. Research felt different. I remember working on some small graphics projects, trying to make simulations of fluids and snow and things like that, and the feeling of not knowing whether it would work, and then seeing something come out on the screen that nobody had quite made before, that was addictive to me.

So I would say I had evidence that I liked the process, even if I couldn't be sure I would like it for five years. I liked building systems, I liked the visual feedback you get in graphics, and I liked the moment when a messy idea starts to make sense. Those were signals.

But I also think the question is a bit backwards. You don't fully know before you start. You pick a direction where the small experiments felt good, and then you keep checking in with yourself. During my PhD at MIT there were long stretches where things didn't work, and I had to ask whether I still enjoyed it. The answer was yes, mostly because I cared about the problem of making simulation and differentiable programming fast and accessible, and because I was lucky to be in a group where people were excited about what we were doing.

So my advice is: don't wait for certainty. Try something small, pay attention to how it feels when it's hard, not just when it's fun, and then make the decision with that information. That's really all I had.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts competitive programming with exploratory graphics projects, but it does not describe a transition from reproducing other researchers’ papers to creating his own paper.

astra-6.text: I don’t think I knew for sure. But I liked working on open-ended problems—trying something, seeing why it didn’t work, and then finding a better approach. That process was enjoyable to me, even when the progress was slow. So a PhD felt like a natural next step. It wasn’t that I knew exactly what research would be like; I wanted to spend more time exploring questions where I didn’t already know the answer.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think I knew for sure. But before starting my PhD, I had already had some experience doing research, and I enjoyed the process of exploring a problem without knowing exactly where it would lead. You try something, it doesn’t work, and then you figure out why. When you finally get something working, that’s very satisfying. So it wasn’t that I knew I would enjoy every part of a PhD, but I had enough experience to feel that research was something I wanted to keep doing.
